Cavity preparation pain

Both small studies report lower pain during cavity preparation. One study is randomized and the pediatric study is not, limiting certainty and generalizability.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Both small studies report lower pain during cavity preparation. One study is randomized and the pediatric study is not, limiting certainty and generalizability.

Summary of the Evidence

Two exact-category human studies are listed: one randomized, possibly sham-controlled trial in 24 participants (88 teeth) and one non-randomized study in 10 children (20 molars). No animal or in-vitro/ex-vivo study is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

Both studies report lower pain during tooth-cavity preparation after LLLT. The interpretation is limited by small samples, uncertain masking/control details in Femiano et al., and inadequately reported parameters in Tanboga et al. Findings remain preliminary (Femiano et al. 2018; Tanboga et al. 2011). In the 24-participant study, 88 teeth were evaluated, so tooth counts exceed the number of independent participants. The database description leaves sham/control details uncertain, and the pediatric study included 20 molars from 10 children without randomization. Both reports address pain during one operative visit, not later recovery, avoidance of anesthesia, or prevention of restorative treatment. The positive signals remain vulnerable to masking, allocation, and within-person clustering; a larger randomized study with prespecified pain and rescue-anesthetic outcomes would be more informative.

Primary original studies: Femiano et al. 2018 Tanboga et al. 2011

Animal evidence

none identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

none identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The reviewed source record identifies low-level diode laser treatment before cavity preparation but does not provide a complete, consistently reported parameter set for both studies. No wavelength or dose is inferred here. Because the reports differ in participants and design, their settings cannot be treated as one shared protocol. Visible red or blue wavelengths and near-infrared wavelengths are distinct bands.

Interpretation

The results concern pain during a single operative visit, not later recovery or avoidance of local anesthesia. Participant-level clustering, masking, and allocation details affect interpretation. Replication with prespecified pain measures and rescue-anesthetic outcomes would be needed to determine whether the observed signal is clinically reliable.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow. Two small studies suggest less pain during cavity preparation, with one non-randomized.
Publications and records2 unique titles.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two small human studies report less pain during cavity preparation after low-level laser treatment. One randomized study includes 88 teeth from 24 participants, so teeth are not independent participants. The pediatric study is non-randomized. Limited samples and incomplete protocol reporting leave the effect preliminary.
